also: a star shooting across the sky

terms.gloss: a falling star, a shooting star
terms.grammar: stēlla, stēllae f. with the present participle of cadō; plural stēllae cadentēs
evidence: Sen. NQ 7.23.2: quae trānsversae dīcuntur stēllae et cadentēs praetervolant et secant āëra
terms.comment: The everyday name, which Seneca reports as what people call them; Vergil’s shooting stars likewise fall or slide from the sky (stēllās … praecipitēs caelō lābī, dē caelō lāpsa … stēlla).

terms.gloss: the shooting of a star across the sky (the event)
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.2: trājectiōnēs mōtūsque stēllārum observitāvērunt
terms.comment: Cicero’s word in the language of omens: the star’s passage, not the star.

terms.gloss: a star darting across the sky
evidence: Sen. NQ 7.23.3: nam et fax et fulmen et stēlla trānscurrēns

phrases.english: Look, a shooting star! Did you see it?

phrases.latin: saepe etiam stēllās ventō impendente vidēbis praecipitēs caelō lābī, noctisque per umbram flammārum longōs ā tergō albēscere tractūs
phrases.english: often too, when wind is coming, you will see stars shoot headlong from the sky, and long trails of flame whiten behind them through the dark of night

phrases.latin: dē caelō lāpsa per umbrās stēlla facem dūcēns multā cum lūce cucurrit
phrases.english: gliding from the sky through the darkness, a star ran across trailing a torch, with a great light

sources: Lewis & Short: stella · Lewis & Short: cado · Lewis & Short: trajectio · Lewis & Short: transcurro
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. meteor, shooting star.
